P01.256
Selective Metabotropic Glutamate Receptor 5
(mGlu,) Antagonism Reduces L-DOPA-Induced
Dyskinesia in MPTP-Lesioned Primates at the
Expense of Anti-Parkinsonian Benefit Tom H.
Johnston, Susan H. Fox, Toronto, ON, Canada, Matthew J. Pig-
gott, Perth, Australia, Jonathan M. Brotchie, Toronto, ON, Can-
ada
OBJECTIVE: To assess whether the potential benefit of anti-dyskinetic
actions of metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGlus) antagonists might be
compromised by loss of anti-parkinsonian efficacy. BACKGROUND:
mGlu, antagonists (e.g. ADX10059 and AFQ056) have been proposed as
one potential means of reducing L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID) in Par-
kinson’s disease (PD). However, for anti-dyskinetic actions to be of maximal
therapeutic benefit they must not be associated with worsening of parkin-
sonian symptoms. Here we assess the effects of the prototypical, selective
mGlu; antagonist, 3-((2-methyl-4-thiazolyl)ethynyl)pyridine (MTEP), in the
MPTP-lesioned macaque model of PD. DESIGN/METHODS: Six parkinso-
nian cynomolgus monkeys were treated with L-DOPA (25 mg/kg p.o. bid)
for 3 months to elicit dyskinesia. After development of stable LID, MTEP
(4.5 — 36 mg/kg, p.o.), or vehicle, was administered alone or in combination
with a dose of L-DOPA defined for each animal as producing maximal
anti-parkinsonian benefit (as MadoparTM, 33 + 1 mg/kg, p.o.). Parkinson-
ism and dyskinesia were assessed by post hoc analysis of DVD-recorded
behaviour by a movement disorder neurologist blinded to treatment. RE-
SULTS: MTEP (18 and 36 mg/kg) significantly reduced peak dose LID (by
63% and 100%). Moreover, MTEP did not reduce total duration of anti-
parkinsonian benefit and indeed increased time “on without disabling dys-
kinesia” (by 70% at 36 mg/kg) and reduced “on time with disabling
dyskinesia” (by 37% at 36 mg/kg). However, the magnitude of anti-
parkinsonian actions of L-DOPA, especially in the first two hours after
administration, was actually reduced by MTEP such that, at 18 and 36
mg/kg, parkinsonism scores were 170% and 160%, respectively, higher than
with L-DOPA alone. CONCLUSIONS/RELEVANCE: While mGlu, antag-
onists have the potential to alleviate LID and increase duration of anti-
parkinsonian benefit without disabling dyskinesia, at the most effective
anti-dyskinetic doses, mGlu; antagonists may reduce the magnitude of
anti-parkinsonian benefit.
Disclosure: Dr. Johnston has nothing to disclose. Dr. Fox has received personal com-

a consultant. Dr. Piggott has nothing to disclose. Dr. Brotchie has received personal

P01.257
Ratings of “Mental Rigidity” Reflect Cholinergic
Rather Than Dopaminergic Denervation in
Parkinson Disease Kelvin L. Chou, Martijn L. Muller, Rob-
ert A. Koeppe, Michael R. Kilbourn, Kirk A. Frey, Roger L. Albin,
Nicolaas I. Bohnen, Ann Arbor, MI
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the relationship between ratings of “mental
rigidity”, cortical cholinergic and nigrostriatal dopaminergic activity in pa-
tients with Parkinson disease (PD). BACKGROUND: Non-motor symp-
toms are common in PD and represent a significant source of disability in
this disorder. Features of a characteristic personality type with introver-
sion, punctuality, and inflexibility have been suggested to be associated
with PD. Using factor analysis technique of a personality and behavioral
questionnaire, we previously derived four factors from a 27-item question-
naire describing various aspects of mental rigidity in patients with PD. The
first factor consisted of 15 high-loading items representing features of men-
tal preoccupation and social viscosity. The second factor had 7 high-loading
items representing symptoms of mental inflexibility. The third factor had 4
relevant items on compulsiveness and impulsiveness. The fourth factor had
4 high-loading items reflecting introversion and social anxiety. DESIGN/
METHODS: Thirty-two male PD subjects (Hoehn and Yahr stages I-III,
mean age 68.9 + 8.0) completed the mental rigidity questionnaire and
underwent !!C-PMP acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and 'C-DTBZ vesicular
monoamine transporter type 2 (VMAT2) PET imaging. RESULTS: Lower
cortical AChE activity correlated with higher ratings on factors 1 (Rs=-
0.60, P=0.0003), 2 (Rs=-0.40, P=0.025), and 4 (Rs=-0.53, P=0.002) but not
factor 3 (Rs=-0.05, ns). There were no significant correlations between
striatal dopamine activity and scores on factors 1 (Rs=0.18, ns), 2 (Rs=-
0.09, ns), 3 (Rs =0.28, ns), or 4 (Rs =0.016, ns). Analysis limited to the
caudate nucleus demonstrated similar results. CONCLUSIONS/RELE-
VANCE: Non-motor symptom ratings of social viscosity, mental inflexibil-
ity, and introversion reflect cholinergic but not nigrostriatal dopaminergic
denervation in PD. In contrast, compulsiveness is not explained by cholin-
ergic denervation. Supported by: Department of Veterans Affairs.

P01.258
Critical Alterations in the Basal Ganglia
Pathophysiology in Parkinson’s Disease. A
Computational Model Approach Georgios Tsirogiannis,
Georgios A. Tagaris, Clementine E. Karageorgiou, Konstantina
Nikita, Athens, Greece
OBJECTIVE: To create a computational model of the basal ganglia and
identify the critical pathophysiological alteration that lead to ‘parkinsonian’
behavior, as depicted from actual recordings from the basal ganglia of
patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD) during deep brain stimulation sur-
gery (DBS). BACKGROUND: Recordings from the basal ganglia of pa-
tients with Parkinson’s disease (PD) have revealed a characteristic beta
band of the subthalamic nucleus’ local field potentials (LFPs). This peak is
thought to be related to the pathophysiology of Parkinson’s disease. We
used a population level computational model of the basal ganglia in an
effort to determine the critical alterations thal lead to the generation of the
beta band. DESIGN/METHODS: The mathematical basis of the model
used in this work has originally been described by Lopes da Silva (1974).
The following projections were incorporated: Cortex to STN, Globus Palli-
dus externa (GPe) to STN, STN to GPe, GPe to GPi; finally, internal
projections within GPe and STN. To assess the proposed model, we used
LFPs recorded from the STN of four patients during typical DBS opera-
tions. RESULTS: Parkinsonian conditions were reproduced by the model
by proper modifications of the strengths of dopamine depleted synapses. Of
particular interest is the suggestion by the model that the beta band is the
consequence of synchronized oscillations of the GPe-STN loop. Specifically,
the tight interplay between the GPe and the STN leads to oscillatory
activity, the specific frequency of which is determined by the values of
synaptic time constants and axonal delays. CONCLUSIONS/RELE-
VANCE: 1. A characteristic beta band peak is identified in the LFP record-
ings from the STN of patients with PD. 2. This finding can be reproduced
by a population level computational model of the basal ganglia. 3. A predic-
tion of the model is that the beta band peak is produced by the tight
interplay between the GPe and the STN. Supported by: The Greek Secre-
tariat of Research and Technology, under grant PENED 03ED512 (2006—
2009).

P01.259
Glycine Receptor Antibodies in Immune-Mediated
Movement Disorders: Progressive
Encephalomyelitis with Rigidity and Myoclonus,
Opsoclonus-Myoclonus Syndrome, and Ocular
Flutter Syndrome Takahiro Iizuka, Yoshiaki Urano, Saori
Miyakawa, Junichi Hamada, Sagamihara, Japan, Maria I. Leite,
Angela Vincent, Oxford, United Kingdom, Fumihiko Sakai, Hideki
Mochizuki, Sagamihara, Japan
OBJECTIVE: To look for glycine receptor antibodies (GlyR-Abs) in three
patients with distinct immune-mediated movement disorders: progressive
encephalomyelitis with myoclonus and rigidity (PERM), opsoclonus-
myoclonus syndrome (OMS), and ocular flutter syndrome (OFS). These
syndromes are considered to be due to an impairment of central inhibitory
circuit with increased excitation of spinal or ocular motoneurons. BACK-
GROUND: GlyR-Abs were recently reported in a case of PERM who had no
antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD-Abs) (Hutchinson M,
et al. Neurology.2008;71:1291). This patient also had marked hyperek-
plexia. We looked for these antibodies in three patients with immune-
mediated syndromes presumably related with impairment of inhibitory
glycinergic transmission. DESIGN/METHODS: GlyR-Abs were examined
in sera/CSF from 3 patients with GAD-Ab-positive PERM without hyperek-
plexia (case 1), postinfectious OMS with hyperekplexia (case 2), and postin-
fectious OFS without hyperekplexia (case 3). The GlyR-Abs were measured
at Oxford using HEK293 cells transfected with EGFP-tagged GlyR alphal
subunit. RESULTS: Case 1 (PERM; a 61-yo woman) presented with pro-
gressive gait difficulty with myoclonic jerks in the lower extremities. She
also had diplopia, nystagmus, lateral gaze palsy, dysphagia, marked neck
rigidity but no cognitive impairment, hyperekplexia or hyperreflexia. GAD-
Abs were positive (34300 U/ml in serum). Case 2 (OMS; a 34-yo-man)
presented with oscillopsia and unsteady gait. He had scanning speech,
opsoclonus, and trembling minimyoclonus, truncal ataxia, marked hyperek-
plexia and hyperreflexia without spasticity. Case 3 (OFS: a 41-yo-woman)
presented with oscillopsia and unsteady gait. She had ocular flutter but no
myoclonus, hyperekplexia or hyperreflexia. All patients improved after

patients with PERM but suggest that they are not necessarily associated

P01.260
Two Parkinson’s Disease Patients with a-
Synuclein Gene Duplication and Rapid Cognitive
Decline Chae Won Shin, Sung Sup Park, Beom Seok Jeon,
Seoul, Republic of Korea
OBJECTIVE: We screened 717 index patients with PD for the presence of
SNCA multiplication. BACKGROUND: We previously reported duplica-
tion of SNCA in two cases of apparently sporadic PD. Subsequently, three
more patients with SNCA duplication without a family history have re-
ported. However, no further reports have been issued concerning SNCA
multiplication in sporadic PD. DESIGN/METHODS: Patients were re-
cruited at the Movement Disorder Clinic at Seoul National University
Hospital. Thirty patients had at least one first-degree relative with parkin-
sonism. SNCA gene dosages were assessed by semi-quantitative multiplex
PCR. RESULTS: The results of semi-quantitative multiplex PCR show
duplication in two patients. The first patient was a 55-year old woman
presented with a rest and postural tremor at age 48. Motor fluctuation and
hallucination was already present when first seen by us at age 50. She
experienced frequent syncope. At age 52, she had an advanced parkinson-
ism with hallucinations, and orthostatic hypotension. Her MMSE was 21/
30. None of her parents or six siblings has features of parkinsonism. The
second patient was a 63-year-old woman whose parkinsonism started with
a tremor at age 55. At age 56, she was diagnosed as PD of HY stage 2.
When first seen by us at age 59, she had HY stage 3 parkinsonism ortho-
static hypotension, and hallucinations. Her MMSE was 17/30. None of her
parents and 6 siblings had parkinsonism. CONCLUSIONS/RELE-
VANCE: In this study, we were able to reaffirm the presence of SNCA
duplication in apparently sporadic PD (2/687=0.3%). Previous studies have
shown that SNCA duplication has a wide clinical spectrum. SNP rs356219
in the 3’-region of SNCA has been shown to be associated with PD. Herein
we screened SNP in total 5 patients and 4 asymptomatic careers. Patients
homozygous for the G allele had an earlier disease onset. We suggest
1s356219*G as a possible modifying factor of the SNCA duplication. Sup-
ported by: Seoul National University Hospital; Grant Number: 03-2008-
015.

PO1.261
Evaluation of SNCA CpG Island Methylation Level
in Post-Mortem Brain of Parkinson’s Disease and
Dementia with Lewy Bodies Lumine Matsumoto, Atsushi
Iwata, Hisatomo Kowa, Yu Nagashima, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, Japan,
Hiroshi Takuma, Akira Tamaoka, Tsukuba-shi, Ibaraki, Japan,
Hiroshi Kurisaki, Kiyose, Tokyo, Japan, Shoji Tsuji, Bunkyo-ku,
Tokyo, Japan
OBJECTIVE: To explore the possibility of involvement of epigenetics in
the pathogenesis of Parkinson’s disease (PD) and Dementia with Lewy
bodies (DLB). BACKGROUND: Epigenetic mechanism including CpG
isand DNA methylation has an important role in regulating the expression
of downstream gene. There are accumulating evidence of aberrant epige-
netical gene regulations in cancer and psychiatric disorders. Epigenetics
might also have effects on neurodegenerative disorders such as PD and
DLB, in which alpha-synuclein gene (SNCA) expression level is suggested
to be related to disease pathogenesis. Methylation of CpG island leads to
downstream gene suppression, while demethylation upregulates the ex-
pression, thus we hypothesized that aberrant demethylation of SNCA CpG
island could be a cause of PD/DLB. DESIGN/METHODS: Genomic DNA
was extracted from post mortem brain of pathologically proven 13 PD/DLB
and 10 non-PD/DLB control patients over 55 years old at the time of death.
Sections were obtained from cingulate cortex (control 6 samples, PD/DLB
12 samples), putamen (control 2, PD/DLB 7) and substatia nigra (control 2,
PD/DLB 3). Bisulfite sequencing of SNCA gene CpG island was performed.
Twelve to 24 clones per samples were analyzed. Percentage of methylation
status of total 13 CpG sites was calculated. RESULTS: The methylation
level of cingulate cortex was 94.7+1.3 % (SE) in controls and 91.7+4.4 % in
PD/DLB, 96.0+3.5 % vs 85.8+7.2 % in putamen and 99+1.1 % vs 0.9+0.4
% in substantia nigra. CONCLUSIONS/RELEVANCE: There was a large
diversity among brain areas in methylation level of human SNCA gene
CpG island. In some areas, methylation levels were lower in PD/DLB pa-
tients compared to controls. Although no statistical significance was de-
tected due to small sample size, the result suggested the possible
involvement of abnormal SNCA CpG methylation in PD/DLB. Supported
by: Ministry of Health, Labour, and Welfare; Ministry of Education, Cul-
ture, Science and Technology; Brain Science Foundation; and Sankyo Foun-
dation of Life Science, Japan.

P01.262
CD-PROBE (Cervical Dystonia Patient Registry for
Observation of BOTOX® Efficacy) — A
Multicenter, Observational Study of Repeated
OnabotulinumtoxinA Injections in Cervical
Dystonia (CD) Patients - Preliminary Baseline
Data Joseph Jankovic, Houston, TX, Charles Adler, Scottsdale,
AZ, David Charles, Nashville, TN, Cynthia Comella, Chicago, IL,
Mark Stacy, Durham, NC, Matthias Kurth, San Diego, CA, Mitch-
ell Brin, Irvine, CA, Lisa Misell, San Diego, CA, Lee M. Boo,
Irvine, CA
OBJECTIVE: Report initial baseline data in a multicenter observational
study of CD. BACKGROUND: The treatment of CD has expanded beyond
neurologists and movement disorder specialists. CD-PROBE is an ongoing
registry intended to better define the use of onabotulinumtoxinA across a
broad range of physicians. DESIGN/METHODS: Multicenter, open-label,
prospective, observational study. Inclusion criteria: a) toxin naive, b) new to
practice or c) if previously participated in botulinum toxin (BoNT) trial,
>16 weeks post last injection. Patients are followed over 3 treatment cycles
and evaluated at time of injection and at 4—6 weeks post-injections. The
following data are collected: practice characteristics/demographics, CD clas-
sification/severity, Toronto Western Spasmodic Torticollis Rating Scale
(TWSTRS), Pain Numeric Rating Scale (pain NRS), Cervical Dystonia Im-
pact Profile (CDIP-58), Healthcare Utilization and Work Productivity Ques-
tionnaire, BoNT/A injection regimens, Clinician and Patient Global
Impression of Change. RESULTS: As of October 19, 2009, 179 patients has
been enrolled (females=77%, males=23%, Caucasians=96%). Mean age at
enrollment is 58+14.8 (20-86) years (retired=34%, full-time em-
ployed=33%, disabled=14% other=19%), with symptoms first noted at
48+17.2 (5-82) years of age. Mean time from symptoms onset to diagnosis
is 6+9.6 (0-48) years and mean time to first treatment is 1+3.0 (0-31)
years after diagnosis. Baseline clinical characteristics: a) TW-
STRS=39.5+1, b) subjective severity classification by physicians:
mild=79, moderate=83, severe=13; c) pain NRS=5.39+2.98, d) CDIP-58
subscale scores: Head and Neck Symptoms=69.2+19.0, Pain and Discom-
fort=71.7+22.8, Upper Limb Activities=53.2+22.4, Walking=44.6+23.5,
Sleep=59.1+26.9, Annoyance=58.2+22.1, Mood=48.7+22.2, Psychosocial
Function=50.4+23.7. Forty-eight patients (26.8%) were previously treated
with BoNT, 5 (2.8%) with surgical intervention and 1 (0.6%) with phenol
injections. CONCLUSIONS/RELEVANCE: CD-PROBE will provide in-
sight into the management of CD in real-world practice. Baseline charac-
teristics suggest that CD is a highly disabling condition. Results of this
study will provide a more complete picture of the impact of onabotulinum-
toxinA on patients disease status, quality of life and work productivity.
Supported by: Allergan, Inc.
